---
title: "Nobody jumps the line"
---

A hairdresser serves whoever has waited longest. Your undo stack does the
opposite: it hands back whatever arrived last, which is exactly right for Ctrl+Z
and exactly wrong for a salon. This chapter builds the structure that keeps a
line fair, with one pointer at each end of the chain, and puts it under a page
where humans and dogs wait for a haircut.

## The stack gets it wrong {#sec-queues-experiment}

1. Open `coursework/train-builder`, the app with your own tested `Stack<T>` in
   `src/stack.ts`. Create `src/salon.test.ts` next to it:

   ```ts
   import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
   import { Stack } from './stack';

   describe('a salon that stores its customers in a stack', () => {
     it('serves the customer who has waited longest', () => {
       const line = new Stack<string>();
       line.push('Anna');
       line.push('Ben');
       line.push('Chiara');

       expect(line.pop()).toBe('Anna');
     });
   });
   ```

2. Anna walked in first, so Anna gets the chair first. That is what the test
   says. Predict what `pop()` really gives back, then run this one file:

   ```text
   npx vitest run src/salon.test.ts
   ```

   ```text
    ❯ src/salon.test.ts (1 test | 1 failed) 6ms
        × serves the customer who has waited longest 5ms

   ⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯ Failed Tests 1 ⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯

    FAIL  src/salon.test.ts > a salon that stores its customers in a stack > serves the customer who has waited longest
   AssertionError: expected 'Chiara' to be 'Anna' // Object.is equality

   Expected: "Anna"
   Received: "Chiara"
   ```

3. Delete `src/salon.test.ts` again. It was a scratch experiment, and the train
   builder's own tests should stay the only tests in that project.

The stack did nothing wrong. Chiara walked in last, so Chiara sits on top of the
chain, and `pop()` takes the top. Last in, first out is the whole point of an
undo history, where the click you want back is always the most recent one. In a
salon the same rule means Chiara gets the chair while Anna, who has been waiting
since ten o'clock, watches her go.

## First in, first out {#sec-queues-fifo}

A structure that hands back the oldest item first is a **queue**, and its rule
is **FIFO**: first in, first out. It is the rule of the supermarket checkout and
of a printer working through the jobs people sent it, and it is the only rule a
waiting line can use without starting an argument.

The two operations get their own names, because `push` and `pop` say nothing
about which end they work on:

* **enqueue** puts an item at the back of the line
* **dequeue** takes the item at the front out of the line and gives it back

The class in this chapter is called `WaitingLine<T>`, and this is everything it
can do:

```ts
class WaitingLine<T> {
  enqueue(item: T): void;
  dequeue(): T | null;
  get length(): number;
  isEmpty(): boolean;
  toArray(): T[];
}
```

`dequeue` gives back `null` when the line is empty, the same answer the playlist
gave for a song it could not find: you asked, and there is nothing there.
`toArray()` lists the customers front first, so `toArray()[0]` is the one in the
chair.

## Two pointers, one line {#sec-queues-tail}

![The line is a chain of nodes. The head pointer holds the customer who is
served next, the tail pointer holds the customer who joined
last.](queue-head-tail.svg){width=560}

A stack gets by with a head pointer, because push and pop both happen at that
one end. A queue works on both ends, and the two ends need different things.

Taking the front customer out is cheap either way: read `head.value`, move
`head` on to `head.next`, done. Adding at the back is the problem. The last node
in the chain is the one whose `next` is `null`, and the only way to reach it
from the head is to walk the whole chain. Ten customers, ten steps. Five hundred
customers, five hundred steps for the next one who walks in. That is the price
`unshift` charges an array for inserting at the front (@sec-linked-list-costs),
turned around and charged at the back.

So the class keeps a second pointer that always holds the last node. The file
starts with the same `Node<T>` you wrote for the playlist and for the stack,
because every app in this part builds its own:

```ts
class Node<T> {
  value: T;
  next: Node<T> | null = null;

  constructor(value: T) {
    this.value = value;
  }
}

export class WaitingLine<T> {
  private head: Node<T> | null = null;
  private tail: Node<T> | null = null;
  private count = 0;
```

The two methods go inside that class. `enqueue` touches two nodes and walks
nowhere:

```ts
  enqueue(item: T): void {
    const node = new Node(item);

    if (this.tail === null) {
      this.head = node;
    } else {
      this.tail.next = node;
    }

    this.tail = node;
    this.count++;
  }
```

`dequeue` works at the other end, and it hands back `null` instead of a value
when there is nobody to serve:

```ts
  dequeue(): T | null {
    if (this.head === null) {
      return null;
    }

    const front = this.head;
    this.head = front.next;

    if (this.head === null) {
      this.tail = null;
    }

    this.count--;
    return front.value;
  }
```

The playlist counted its songs by walking the chain on every read
(@sec-iteration-length). This class keeps a `count` field instead. Only two
methods ever change the line, so keeping the number honest costs one line in
each of them, and the page reads `length` every single time it redraws.

## The line with one customer in it {#sec-queues-edge-cases}

The `if` at the top of `enqueue` and the `if` in the middle of `dequeue` are the
whole reason a queue is more than a chain with two pointers. Both of them are
about a line that holds exactly one customer, reached from the two directions.

![An empty line has both pointers on null, the first enqueue puts both pointers
on the same node, and the dequeue that hands that customer out puts both back on
null.](queue-edge-cases.svg){width=520}

When Ida walks into an empty salon there is no last node to attach her to, so
`this.tail.next = node` would crash on a `null`. She becomes the first customer
and the last one at the same time, which is why the empty case sets `head` and
the line below sets `tail`.

When Ida walks out again, `head` moves on to `head.next`, and for the last
customer that is `null`. Forget the second `if` and `tail` still points at Ida,
who has left the building. Nothing goes wrong yet. The page shows an empty line,
`isEmpty()` asks the head and says `true`, and the bug sits there and waits. It
shows up on the next `enqueue`: the new node gets hooked behind Ida, `head` stays
`null`, and the customer disappears into a chain nobody can reach.

A bug that needs three steps to become visible is exactly what a test file is
for. Among the tests you copy in for the exercise, one is called `takes new
items again`: it enqueues one item, dequeues it, and then enqueues two more.
That is the only test in the file that a forgotten `tail = null` turns red.

::: {.research title="Two things the exercise needs"}
The Add human form has a Long hair checkbox, and the test file you copy in
carries three tests that do not test anything yet. This chapter answers neither
question, and the exercise needs both answers.

1. A checkbox is an `<input type="checkbox">`, and in TypeScript it is an
   `HTMLInputElement` like every other input. Reading `.value` on it gives you
   the string `'on'` whether the box is ticked or not. Which property answers
   whether it is ticked, and what type does that property have? MDN has a page
   for `HTMLInputElement`.
2. The three unwritten tests all say `expect.fail('Test not implemented yet')`.
   What does `expect.fail` do when the test runs, and why would the author of a
   test file put it there on purpose? The Vitest documentation for `expect` has
   the answer.

For the exam, the checkbox property has to be in your head. Reading a form and
turning it into an object is the first half of half the exercises you will get.
:::

## Exercise: the salon waiting line {#sec-queues-exercise}

{{< exercise hairdresser tests=true >}}

1. Create a new app from our tests template inside `coursework/`, in a folder
   called `hairdresser`. Part 8 comes back to this app, so give the folder
   exactly that name.

2. Delete `src/math.ts` and `src/math.test.ts`. The files you copy in bring
   their own `index.html` and their own `src/index.ts`.

3. Run `npx tsc --noEmit` and read what it says:

   ```text
   src/waiting-line.ts(13,11): error TS6133: 'head' is declared but its value is never read.
   src/waiting-line.ts(15,11): error TS6133: 'tail' is declared but its value is never read.
   src/waiting-line.ts(21,11): error TS6133: 'item' is declared but its value is never read.
   ```

   Those three complaints are your to-do list. Every method in
   `src/waiting-line.ts` throws `new Error('Method not implemented.')`, so
   nothing in the file uses the two pointers yet, and TypeScript refuses to let
   a field or a parameter sit there unread.

4. Write `Human` and `Dog` in `src/customer.ts`. Both extend the `Customer`
   class that is already there, both implement `describe()`, and the strings
   have to match to the character:

   * `🧑 Mia Berger (long hair)` for a human with long hair
   * `🧑 Tom Novak (short hair)` for a human without
   * `🐕 Rex (Beagle)` for a dog

   A human is built from a first name, a last name, and whether the hair is
   long. A dog is built from a name and a breed. Parameter properties keep both
   classes down to a constructor and one method.

5. Write the five members of `WaitingLine<T>`. `enqueue` and `dequeue` are in
   @sec-queues-tail. `isEmpty()` asks the head. `toArray()` starts at the head
   and follows `next` until it runs out, pushing every value into an array, front
   first. `length` gives back the counter.

6. Run `npm test`:

   ```text
    ❯ src/waiting-line.test.ts (16 tests | 3 failed) 8ms
          × puts the first item at the front and at the back of the line 2ms
          × makes the line non-empty 0ms
          × keeps the first item at the front while the newest joins the back 0ms
   ```

   ```text
    Test Files  1 failed (1)
         Tests  3 failed | 13 passed (16)
   ```

   Thirteen tests already pass against the class you just wrote. If any of them
   is red, fix the class before you go on.

7. Write the three missing tests in `src/waiting-line.test.ts`. Each one has a
   comment above it saying what it has to show. `head` and `tail` are private,
   so a test cannot look at them and does not need to: `toArray()`, `length`,
   and `isEmpty()` say everything about the line from the outside. When all
   three are written you get:

   ```text
    Test Files  1 passed (1)
         Tests  16 passed (16)
   ```

8. Open `src/index.ts` and replace the six `TODO` comments. Two of them ask the
   customer at the front and the one behind them to `describe()` themselves, two
   build a `Human` and a `Dog` from the form and enqueue them, one clears the
   checkbox after a human joined, and the last one dequeues when Serve next is
   clicked. The element lookups, the render helper, and the two `submit`
   listeners with their empty-field checks are already wired.

9. Run `npm start` and walk through the salon. Expected results:

   * the fresh page shows `The line is empty.`, `Customers in line: 0`, and a
     gray Serve next button
   * add Mia Berger with Long hair ticked, then Rex the Beagle, then Tom Novak
     with the box empty: the page shows
     `Now serving: 🧑 Mia Berger (long hair)`, `Next up: 🐕 Rex (Beagle)`, and
     `Customers in line: 3`
   * click Serve next: `Now serving: 🐕 Rex (Beagle)` and
     `Next up: 🧑 Tom Novak (short hair)`
   * click it twice more: the line is empty again and the button turns gray
   * click Add human with both name fields empty:
     `Please enter a first name and a last name.` appears and nobody joins

10. Add the `verify` script with its three checks to `package.json` as in every
    new app, run `npm run verify`, fix what it reports, and commit.

::: {.callout-tip}
## From last year's exam sheet

"No arrays and no built-in structures inside the line, the job is to build the
chain yourself. And the class stays generic: `WaitingLine` never mentions
`Customer`."

The second sentence is the one people lose points on. It is tempting to type
`enqueue(item: Customer)` when the only app you can see holds customers, and the
test file settles the question for you: it fills the same class with strings and
with numbers, and a `WaitingLine` that knows about haircuts fails all of it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## When you finish early

**Test the customers too.** `src/customer.test.ts`, three `it` blocks, one per
line of text from step 4. They are the cheapest tests in the project and they
catch the missing space in `(long hair)`.

**Show the whole line.** `toArray()` already hands you every customer in order.
Render the ones behind the first two into an `<ol>` under Next up, and give the
list item of the last customer a class so you can gray it out in CSS.

**Count the served customers.** Keep a number next to the line, add one to it in
the Serve next listener, and show `Served today: 4` under the count. Nothing in
`WaitingLine` changes for this, which is the point: the queue hands out
customers and has no opinion about what you do with them.
:::
